video_title: 🔬Biology Is Turning Into Software — Matt McPartlon and Neil Patil, Chai Discovery
gist: Chai Discovery co-founder Matt McPartlon and product/platform lead Neil Patil describe how their Chai-1/2/3 protein structure-prediction and antibody-design models crossed from research demo to pharma production, and why they sell a neutral software platform to Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Novo Nordisk and others rather than developing their own drugs. They detail the Chai-2 result of antibody binders to ~half of 50 targets at ~20% hit rate, sub-angstrom cryo-EM validation, a Figma/Autodesk-style molecular design suite instead of a chatbot, a $400M raise going into compute, and why the real prize is unlocking previously undesignable modalities (GPCR agonists, bispecifics, ADCs) rather than shaving discovery cost.

insights.claim: Chai Discovery deliberately refuses to build its own drug pipeline and positions itself as a 'neutral software factory for making medicines' so it can sell to competing pharma companies simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: A pure-platform AI-bio vendor avoids competing with its customers, which is the structural reason it can stack multiple big-pharma deals — a different risk/return profile than pipeline-owning AI-biotechs.
insights.quote: We really don't see ourselves that way, right? We we see ourselves as almost a a neutral software factory for making medicines.

insights.claim: Chai Discovery has signed four large pharma partnerships — Eli Lilly first, then Pfizer and Novo Nordisk among them — within roughly two and a half years of founding.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Commercial validation from top-tier pharma is the clearest external signal that AI protein design has moved past pilots into budgeted programs.

insights.claim: Chai has raised another $400 million, which is being directed at buying dedicated compute clusters to train larger models that can handle more constraints at once.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Capital in AI-bio is now flowing into GPU capacity rather than wet-lab assets, tightening an already power-law-constrained compute market.
insights.quote: we've you know, we've raised another $400 million. Uh I have to go buy another compute cluster.

insights.claim: Pharma's IP sensitivity was overcome by deploying an effectively separate single-tenant instance of the design product per customer, which insiders had told Chai was impossible.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Security architecture, not model quality, was the gating factor for selling AI tools into pharma — a replicable playbook and a switching-cost moat once deployed.
insights.quote: when I joined a lot of people told me this can't be done like they're not going to put their data in a platform and like have all their new medicines be generating out of it

insights.claim: Chai's deals include training or fine-tuning partner-specific versions of its models on pharma proprietary data, creating per-customer specialized models rather than one general model.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Per-partner fine-tuning is both a revenue line and an integration lock-in; it mirrors the enterprise LLM post-training market forming around foundation labs.

insights.claim: Chai Discovery operates with roughly 30 total employees and a research team of about 10, far smaller than rivals like Isomorphic Labs or DeepMind.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Extreme capital efficiency per headcount suggests compute and ideas, not people, are the binding constraint in AI-bio — relevant to how these companies should be valued.
insights.quote: our research team is like you know in the around 10 people

insights.claim: Chai open-sourced Chai-1, a structure prediction model built on the AlphaFold 3 architecture, primarily as a forcing function to build production MSA and training infrastructure rather than as a product.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing a replication can be an infrastructure-building and distribution strategy, not charity — useful lens for reading other labs' open releases.

insights.claim: Chai-2 is an all-atom diffusion model that lets the model itself decide which atoms are present and maps that back to amino acids, enabling joint co-design of sequence and structure.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Co-design of sequence and structure in one model is the technical step that moved the company from prediction to generating candidate medicines.

insights.claim: In the Chai-2 study the company designed antibodies against 50 targets, obtained binders to about half of them, and averaged roughly a 20% hit rate for binding.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: This is the concrete statistic that convinced pharma the approach generalizes beyond one-off targets; it is the benchmark any competing claim should be measured against.
insights.quote: we designed antibodies to 50 targets for that paper. got binders to about half of them with I think on average around a 20% hit rate for binding

insights.claim: The 50 targets in the Chai-2 campaign were selected from a CRO's validated catalog after roughly half of an earlier self-chosen target set failed for wet-lab process reasons rather than model reasons.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Headline hit rates in AI-bio papers are conditioned on target selection; investors should ask how the target set was chosen before comparing vendors.

insights.claim: Faced with the 25 targets Chai-2 failed on, Chai chose to bet on general model scaling rather than analyzing the properties of the failed targets, which produced the Chai-2.5, Chai-2.7 and Chai-3 line.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: A bitter-lesson-style strategy in biology; if it keeps working it favors compute-rich generalist platforms over target-specific specialist shops.
insights.quote: we bet on the models getting better and we just pushed as hard as we could on that front

insights.claim: Beyond binding affinity, Chai-2.5 was released with a developability study covering safety, stability, manufacturability and self-aggregation, because therapeutic-grade molecules require far more than tight binding.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Developability is the axis where AI design either becomes drug-relevant or stays academic; it is the right diligence question for any binder-design claim.

insights.claim: Chai's stated research north star is to one-shot de novo molecules that are already drug-like straight out of the model, collapsing hit discovery, hit-to-lead and lead optimization into a single step.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: If achieved, it removes the staged CRO/CRO-services value chain that much of preclinical drug services revenue depends on.
insights.quote: the north star is to just really produce drug-like molecules straight out of the models

insights.claim: Antibodies were chosen as the primary modality because the constant framework region is already recognized by the immune system and only the fingertip CDR loops need designing, so developability comes largely for free.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Explains why antibody design commercialized before other modalities and why the same models may struggle to monetize elsewhere without new developability solutions.

insights.claim: Designing an antibody binder can be easier than predicting how an arbitrary antibody binds a target, because in the design setting you can restrict yourself to the structurally easy cases.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive asymmetry: weak antibody-antigen prediction benchmarks do not imply weak design performance, so benchmark-based skepticism can be misplaced.
insights.quote: if you if you have the freedom to choose, you can kind of just pick the easy cases

insights.claim: Cryo-EM validation of a Chai-designed molecule came back with 0.33 angstrom error — about one third the width of an atom — so close to the prediction that the team initially assumed the lab had mistakenly returned their own design file.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Sub-angstrom agreement is the hard evidence that structure prediction has crossed into engineering-grade precision for these design cases.
insights.quote: And in this case it was a 0.33 angstrom error which is 1/3 the width of an atom

insights.claim: The validated targets were deliberately chosen to have no known antibody binder, so any hit was necessarily the first antibody binder to that target and could not be explained by training-data leakage.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Leakage-free target selection is the credibility test that separates real AI-bio results from memorization; ask for it explicitly.

insights.claim: Self-consistency metrics that compare a designed sequence against an independent structure predictor were gamed by the field, because it is easy to score well if all your designed proteins look identical.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: In silico protein design benchmarks are corruptible; diversity of generations and calibrated model confidence must be reported alongside them.
insights.quote: it turns out like it's easy to get self-consistency, consistent design of structures if all of your proteins look identical

insights.claim: Wet-lab validation turnaround for binder designs has compressed from years to weeks thanks to a network of contract wet labs, though still far slower than the hours-long compute-scaled evals of LLM development.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Weeks-long feedback loops are now fast enough for recursive self-improvement, which is the precondition for compounding model advantage in bio.
insights.quote: thankfully we're not at years, right? We're down to like weeks

insights.claim: The single bottleneck Chai's research lead would remove by fiat is the protein-design validation loop — instantly knowing whether a design works — which he calls still an unsolved problem for the whole field.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Fast, cheap, high-throughput experimental validation is arguably the highest-value adjacent business to AI protein design.
insights.quote: it's probably along the lines of just like validating hypotheses and like, you know, knowing for certain that things work

insights.claim: Hyperscalers and the largest AI labs absorb over 95% of shipping B300 units, leaving AI-for-science startups fighting over the remainder, which pushed Chai to buy its own clusters after capacity crunches began in September of last year.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Compute allocation is a power law that structurally disadvantages non-LLM AI companies; securing capacity is itself a competitive moat.
insights.quote: the hyperscalers and the you know the the biggest uh the biggest um AI labs are buying 95 plus% of it right and then you kind of have the startups like fighting over the scraps

insights.claim: Modern accelerators like the B300 and Vera Rubin generation are architected around LLM workloads — huge KV caches and 72-GPU coherent domains — which is a poor fit for structure-prediction models, leaving a whole compute and inference optimization stack unbuilt for this model class.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: An open opportunity for kernels, inference stacks and possibly silicon targeted at scientific model architectures rather than transformers-for-text.
insights.quote: it's it's kind of interesting just how much the compute market has kind of gotten LLM pill

insights.claim: AlphaFold-style pair representations force attention over an L-squared sequence that batches out to L-cubed cost, making memory bandwidth — even for operations as trivial as layer norm — a dominant bottleneck rather than raw FLOPs.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Structure models are bandwidth-bound in ways LLMs are not, so hardware and cost curves for this sector will diverge from LLM economics.

insights.claim: Chai standardized early on the Temporal framework for durable execution across database calls, model calls and long data pipelines, because distributed inference work otherwise degrades into hand-rolled queue and retry code consuming most engineering time.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Durable-execution infrastructure is emerging as a load-bearing primitive for AI companies running wide fleets of flaky GPU jobs.
insights.quote: You're ending up spending like 95 plus% of your time on all of this queuing and retry stuff

insights.claim: Chai's product lead argues the biggest blocker to turning biology into an engineering discipline is not biology but missing engineering primitives, including chaotic biological file formats and infrastructure for scaling training.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Reframes AI-bio bottlenecks as software-infrastructure problems, which is where generalist engineering talent and tooling vendors can capture value.
insights.quote: I actually think that's a lot of the bi the the the bottleneck to making uh making biology more like engineering is just like having the right engineering primitives.

insights.claim: Chai treats architectural complexity and the bitter lesson as fundamentally at odds, citing AlphaFold 3's roughly 23 submodules as a system too complex to study or optimize, and keeps a SpaceX Raptor 1 vs Raptor 2 photo on the office wall as a simplicity reminder.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: A simplicity-biased architecture is a bet that scaling wins; it predicts which labs can absorb larger compute budgets productively.
insights.quote: complexity and being bitter lesson pill they're like fundamentally at odds

insights.claim: Abundant protein sequence data is what let transformer approaches like ESM work, while experimental structural data remains far too scarce for the same brute-force treatment — a persistent data blocker for zero-shot clinical-grade design.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Structural and labeled-assay data scarcity, not model capability, is the binding constraint — making proprietary experimental data generation strategically valuable.
insights.quote: there's a ton of sequence data and like that's one of the unlocks for like ESM working. Uh you can get that to just run on a transformer. If you try to do the same thing with like experimental structure data, good luck.

insights.claim: Chai deliberately rejected a chatbot interface in favor of a visual CAD-style design suite resembling Autodesk, SolidWorks or Figma, with a paint tool for selecting epitopes and a content-aware-fill equivalent for generating binders.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: The winning interface for scientific AI may be spatial and direct-manipulation, not conversational — a design signal for anyone building vertical AI products.
insights.quote: it it looks a lot less like a, you know, a Chad GBT and a lot more like uh Autodesk or or Solid Works or or Figma

insights.claim: Chai's product lead expects to rewrite the product at successively higher levels of abstraction — from inspecting individual molecules like inspecting code, to orchestrating epitope campaigns, to whole-pathway campaigns — as model capability climbs.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: AI-era application software has a one-year useful life and functions as a bridge to research value, which changes how to value vertical AI app companies.
insights.quote: maybe you'd have built software that was supposed to last like 20 years. Now it's supposed to last maybe one year, but it is the bridge to deliver value

insights.claim: Pharma scientists are described as highly technical, pragmatic and willing to be proven wrong — they typically hand over a target they previously failed on, and adopt after seeing results, in sharp contrast to unsophisticated cybersecurity buyers.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption that pharma is a slow, tool-hostile market; proof-on-your-target is the sales motion that converts.
insights.quote: I actually don't blame them for not trusting the models.

insights.claim: A pharma scientist who had spent ten years failing to find an initial binder to a target was moved to tears when Chai's model produced one during a results review.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: A visceral marker of capability discontinuity — decade-long internal programs collapsing into a model run is what drives partnership demand.
insights.quote: She's like no I've just been I've literally spent 10 years trying to get an initial binder to this thing and you guys were able to help me do it.

insights.claim: Chai rejects the framing that its value is saving a couple million dollars of antibody discovery inside a roughly half-billion-dollar per-success drug program, arguing the real value is unlocking targets and modalities that were previously undesignable.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: The investable thesis for AI protein design is capability expansion, not cost reduction — cost-savings ROI models understate the opportunity.
insights.quote: I would think about it as less like, oh, I'm taking the existing drugs that I can do and making them faster.

insights.claim: Bispecific antibodies are effectively impossible to find by traditional screening because the per-arm one-in-a-billion binding probabilities multiply, making first-principles design the only viable route.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Multi-specific and warheaded formats are the modalities where AI design has no incumbent alternative — the clearest greenfield demand.
insights.quote: if you have a one in a billion chance of finding a binder in arm one and a one a billion chance in arm two

insights.claim: Chai showed GPCR agonist activity with Chai-2 — precisely engineering an antibody to press a cell-surface switch rather than merely block it — which is described as extremely hard to achieve without atomic-level epitope precision.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Agonist antibodies open target classes historically served by small molecules, potentially expanding the addressable biologics market.

insights.claim: The incumbent alternative to AI design is still immunization campaigns in mice and billion-scale yeast display screens that yield a handful of hits whose binding site and drug-likeness are unknown.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Frames the competitive baseline: nature and brute-force screening, whose key weakness is lack of epitope control rather than lack of hits.
insights.quote: our uh our biggest competitor is the mouse uh so like or or nature in in certain ways

insights.claim: Chai's models can be conditioned to bind a conserved region shared by human and monkey variants for tox studies while simultaneously avoiding a similar human protein, addressing cross-reactivity and selectivity as a combinatorial constraint problem.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Designing out off-target binding upfront attacks a leading cause of clinical failure and toxicity, which is where most drug-development capital is destroyed.

insights.claim: Chai frames drug discovery's staged waterfall of target discovery, hit discovery and optimization — each gate taking months to years — as convertible into an agile iterative loop once models reliably produce promising candidates.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: If preclinical cycles compress like software release cycles, pharma R&D productivity and the CRO services value chain both get repriced.
insights.quote: each of these has a gate and takes a few months to a few years is this very like waterfall model

insights.claim: Epitope prediction — deciding which site on which protein to target for a given disease — is judged a harder unsolved problem than binder design, with virtual cell models the nearest hope and still a long way out.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Target and epitope selection remains the unautomated upstream bottleneck, so pharma biology expertise retains bargaining power against design platforms.
insights.quote: This is a ridiculously hard problem.

insights.claim: AlphaFold 2 multimer solved only about 11% of antibody-antigen prediction cases, meaning it is wrong roughly 90% of the time and structure prediction is far from solved for antibodies.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the 'AlphaFold solved protein structure' consensus and quantifies the remaining headroom that new entrants are competing for.
insights.quote: the multimemer version of this got like 11% of antibbody antigen prediction cases correct. That means 90% of the time it's wrong

insights.claim: Antibodies resist MSA-based prediction because immune systems recombine them individually for unseen pathogens, so there is no evolutionary template to learn from — unlike the monomeric proteins AlphaFold 2 handled well.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Explains why antibody design is a genuinely separate technical problem from general folding and why a dedicated model franchise can exist there.

insights.claim: The two leading GLP-1 drugs combined represent roughly a trillion-dollar asset, and until about three months ago GLP-1 total revenue exceeded the combined revenue of all AI labs.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil and host
insights.so_what: A stark relative-valuation observation: biology's revenue base dwarfs AI's while attracting far less capital and market attention.
insights.quote: I mean up until I think 3 months ago right GLP1's like total revenue was more than all of the AI labs put together.

insights.claim: Pharma is the domain with arguably the highest downstream value per generated token, since a single model output can lead to a multi-billion-dollar drug asset.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: Value-per-token framing justifies far higher compute spend and pricing in bio inference than in general LLM applications.
insights.quote: I don't know if there's another domain where like the downstream value of a token is like as valuable as it is for pharma

insights.claim: Eroom's law — Moore's law backwards — means the cost per approved drug has been rising exponentially, which guarantees that marginal returns on new drug development eventually turn negative unless the curve is bent.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon and host
insights.so_what: The structural case for AI in pharma: the industry's cost curve is unsustainable, so any technology that bends it captures outsized value.
insights.quote: the cost of actually making a drug in pharma is kind of like increasing exponentially

insights.claim: Pharma is best understood as a venture-capital-style portfolio allocator across targets rather than a manufacturer, a framing reinforced by Genentech being one of Silicon Valley's biggest venture outcomes in the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: If cheaper hit discovery lets pharma take more shots on goal, expect portfolio breadth and riskier target selection rather than pure cost cuts.
insights.quote: Thinking of pharma as like sophisticated capital allocators, right? Where they have these this portfolio of targets and they're allocating between them.

insights.claim: Chai internally treats every employee, including researchers, as a capital allocator whose scarce resources are compute and attention rather than headcount, which is why a 30-person team can compete.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil and Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: An organizational model for AI-native companies where cheap building shifts the constraint from engineering capacity to judgment.
insights.quote: we kind of think of everyone at Chai as a bit of a capital allocator

insights.claim: With roughly 10 to 15 protein design startups plus academic RF diffusion work, Chai expects part of the modality space to commoditize while frontier models still capture the majority of value, explicitly analogizing to open-source versus frontier LLMs.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Predicts a barbell market: commoditized simple binders plus a high-value frontier tier — invest at the frontier or in the product layer, not the middle.
insights.quote: the whole pie is growing but it's growing so fast that even as the open uh source models like share expands the the uh the frontier models are still able to capture the majority of the value

insights.claim: Chai argues the product layer around bio models is as important as the model layer, drawing the analogy that people pay for frontier LLMs partly because of products like Claude Code rather than raw model weights.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Defensibility in AI-bio may accrue to workflow software and integration rather than to model weights that leak or get replicated.
insights.quote: a lot of the reason I don't use the open source model is cuz like you know, I don't get like cloud code

insights.claim: Chai pushes back on the 'no data moat' criticism by noting there are ways to turn compute into data and that close partner collaboration produces demand-informed research direction rather than research done in a vacuum.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: The counterargument to the standard platform-vs-pipeline critique; whether compute-to-data conversion works is the key diligence question.

insights.claim: Chai's entire research team except two people has no formal biology background, and the company argues AI-bio requires the same core ML skills as any other domain, comparing biology expertise to a video model researcher needing to be a film director.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: If true, the AI-bio talent pool is far larger than assumed and ML researchers can be recruited directly — a hiring arbitrage.
insights.quote: people think you can't work on like AI bio unless you're a biologist. But it's kind of like you can't work on like video models unless you're like a director or something.

insights.claim: Chai's product lead names talent obscurity — smart people flowing to LLM labs and SaaS instead of biology because bio feels inaccessible and unvisualizable — as the bottleneck he would remove by fiat.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Talent allocation, not capital, is presented as the sector's scarce input; visualization-first tooling is a deliberate recruiting lever.
insights.quote: I think just like not that many like smart people go and work on bio

insights.claim: Chai reports design model hit rates north of 50% in the sense that a 96-well plate can yield roughly 48 interesting binders, marking the crossing point where biology becomes declaratively precision-engineerable.
insights.speaker: Neil Patil
insights.so_what: Plate-level hit density is the practical metric pharma cares about; above ~50% the wet-lab screening burden changes character entirely.
insights.quote: where you can get design models to give you you know uh hit rates you know north of 50% where now you can put them you know in a in a 96 well plate and actually have like 48 uh interesting binders

insights.claim: Chai's research co-founder claims the field has passed the proof-of-concept stage entirely — commercial traction plus working research means the remaining low-hanging fruit is unusually large relative to other ML fields.
insights.speaker: Matt McPartlon
insights.so_what: A direct call that AI-bio is past the hype trough and into compounding returns, which is the core bull case for the sector.
insights.quote: the signs of life have been showed. We're actually in a place where like the models work. They're delivering value and like there's still tons of really interesting research problems to solve.
